sections.h: Jacob in Jubilees: the blameless son
sections.b: Jubilees (an Ethiopian Orthodox book of Scripture, outside other Bibles) retells Jacob's life so that he has nothing to be ashamed of. He buys the birthright openly for a stated price, with an oath (Jubilees 24:3–7). He has never been with a woman at sixty-three and vows to marry only within the family (Jubilees 25:4–10). At his father's bedside he never says "I am Esau," only "I am your son" (Jubilees 26:13, 19), and heaven itself takes away Isaac's discernment (Jubilees 26:18). He will not leave his old father without permission (Jubilees 27:6), Isaac calls him "upright," "blameless" and "faithful" (Jubilees 27:17), and from beyond the Jordan he sends his parents food four times a year (Jubilees 29:15–20). The peeled branches of Genesis 30 and the wrestling at the Jabbok of Genesis 32 are both left out. Genesis, by contrast, shows Jacob's faults openly, and God's grace working through them.

uncommon: Jubilees (24:7) states outright that Jacob "became the elder" when he bought the birthright, something Genesis leaves the reader to infer.

sections.b: Jubilees darkens Esau at every turn. He sells his birthright after thinking it over "in his heart" (Jubilees 24:4); his Canaanite wives are given to "sexual immorality and lust" (Jubilees 25:1); he presses Jacob for twenty-two years to marry one of their sisters (Jubilees 25:8). Isaac's word to him ends not with freedom, as in Genesis 27:40, but with doom: when he throws off Jacob's yoke he will commit "a sin that is wholly for death" (Jubilees 26:34). He wishes for his father's death (Jubilees 26:35), takes his father's flocks and leaves him alone (Jubilees 29:18). The picture agrees with the New Testament's warning about Esau (Hebrews 12:16–17).
sections.refs: Jubilees 24:4; Jubilees 25:1; Jubilees 25:8; Jubilees 26:34–35; Jubilees 29:18; Genesis 27:40; Hebrews 12:16–17

sections.b: Jubilees ends Isaac's time in Gerar with a curse that Genesis does not have. After his servants find no water following his oath to Abimelech (Jubilees 24:25, reading Genesis 26:32 with "not"), Isaac realizes he swore "under pressure" and curses the Philistines "for the day of wrath and fury": the Kittim and "the righteous people" will root them out, and no place in sky, earth or Sheol will hide them (Jubilees 24:28–32, built on Amos 9:2–4). The angel says the curse is engraved on the heavenly tablets (Jubilees 24:33). R. H. Charles (1902) thought the passage reflects the Maccabean wars against Ashdod (Azotus in 1 Maccabees), Gaza and Ekron (1 Maccabees 10:84–89; 1 Maccabees 11:61–62).

sections.h: Dinah in Jubilees: the law against marrying out
sections.b: Jubilees 30 retells Genesis 34 as the founding story of a law. Dinah is "a little girl, twelve years old" who is carried off, not a young woman who "went out" (Jubilees 30:2; Genesis 34:1). The circumcision of the Shechemites is left out entirely, so the massacre is not a broken promise but heaven's decree (Jubilees 30:3–6). From the story the angel draws a law: a father who gives his daughter to a Gentile is to be stoned, the woman burned, with no atonement (Jubilees 30:7–10). Simeon and Levi's deed "was counted to them as righteousness" (Jubilees 30:17), where Genesis has Jacob curse their anger (Genesis 49:5–7). Judith 9:2 praises the same deed.

Jubilees gives Levi's line the priesthood as a reward for zeal: because Levi avenged Dinah, "The offspring of Levi were chosen for the priesthood and to be Levites, to serve before the Lord as we do," the angels say (Jubilees 30:18). Later Isaac, by a spirit of prophecy, blesses Levi before Judah: his sons will serve "like the angels of the presence," be "rulers, princes and chiefs," teach God's ways and bless Israel, and eat at the Lord's table (Jubilees 31:13–17). This joins the priestly praise of Deuteronomy 33:8–11 and Malachi 2:4–7 with the Phinehas pattern (Numbers 25:13). Charles (1902) saw the Hasmonean priest-rulers behind the priest who also rules.

sections.h: Marriage with the nations in Jubilees
sections.b: Jubilees forbids every marriage between Israelites and Gentiles. Rebekah warns Jacob against Canaanite wives (Jubilees 25:1–3), Isaac repeats it (Jubilees 27:10), and after Shechem the angel declares that a father who gives his daughter to a Gentile is to be stoned and the woman burned, because this is giving one's offspring to Molech (Jubilees 30:7–10). Israel will not be "clean of this uncleanness," and a people that looks away will be judged together (Jubilees 30:14–15). The Torah's ban concerns the nations of Canaan and the danger of idolatry (Deuteronomy 7:3–4); Ezra and Nehemiah applied it more widely (Ezra 9:1–2; Nehemiah 13:23–27). Jubilees goes further than all of them.

sections.h: Molech as marriage to a Gentile (Jubilees)
sections.b: Jubilees 30:10 says a man who gives his daughter to a Gentile "has given some of his offspring to Molech." It reads Leviticus 18:21, "Do not hand over any of your children to make them pass over to Molech," as a ban on marrying a child to a foreigner. R. H. Charles (1902) shows that Targum Pseudo-Jonathan reads the verse the same way, while the Mishnah (Megillah 4:9) orders that anyone who translates it so must be silenced. The Latin version of Jubilees, as Charles reports it, has "to a foreigner" in place of "to Molech."

Jubilees tells Levi's zeal at Shechem in the words used of Phinehas. Phinehas's killing of an Israelite and a Midianite woman "was reckoned to him as righteousness" (Psalm 106:31) and won "a covenant of priesthood for all time, because he was zealous for his God" (Numbers 25:13). Of Simeon and Levi Jubilees says "It was counted to them as righteousness" (Jubilees 30:17), and Levi's offspring are chosen for the priesthood "because he was zealous" (Jubilees 30:18). In both stories zeal against a marriage with outsiders founds a priestly line.

Isaac blesses Judah after Levi: "Be a ruler, you and one of your sons, over Jacob's sons," and "in you the salvation of Israel will be found" (Jubilees 31:18–19). R. H. Charles (1902) thought "one of your sons" points to a messiah from Judah, and noted that the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs look for a leader from Levi (Testament of Levi 18) or from Judah (Testament of Judah 24). In Jubilees the priest is blessed first (Jubilees 31:12–13). Christians see both offices joined in Jesus, from Judah (Hebrews 7:14) and priest "after the pattern of Melchizedek" (Hebrews 7:17).

In Jubilees Jacob reaches Luz on New Year's Day, dreams of the stairway and calls the place "the house of the Lord" (Jubilees 27:19–26), and vows a tenth (Jubilees 27:27). Years later he purifies his household, destroys the foreign gods and goes up to Bethel on the first day of the seventh month to pay the vow (Jubilees 31:1–3), bringing Rebekah and her nurse Deborah (Jubilees 31:30). Chapter 32 continues with Levi's ordination and the tithes there.

Jubilees turns family stories into marriage law. Rebekah, then Isaac, charge Jacob to marry within the family (Jubilees 25:1–3; Jubilees 27:9–10). When Laban gives Leah first, the angel declares from the heavenly tablets that no father may give a younger daughter before an older one, and that guilt is recorded in heaven against anyone who does (Jubilees 28:6–7). Charles (1902) notes that no other Jewish tradition knows this rule, and that Jubilees says nothing of Leviticus 18:18, which forbids marrying two sisters together.

Jubilees 29:9–11 explains that Gilead was once "the land of the Rephaim," giants ten down to seven cubits tall (about fifteen to ten and a half feet), whose royal cities were Karnaim and Ashtaroth, Edrei, Misur and Beon. The Lord destroyed them for their evil, and the Amorites who took their place have filled up their sins. The Bible knows the Rephaim of Bashan and Og, "the last of the Rephaim" (Genesis 14:5; Deuteronomy 2:11; Deuteronomy 3:11). Charles (1902) linked Karnaim and Beon with Judas Maccabee's campaigns (1 Maccabees 5:4–5, 43–44, where the site has Carnaim and Baean).

Jubilees multiplies the family blessings of Genesis. Rebekah, moved by "a spirit of righteousness," lays her hands on Jacob and blesses him with twelve sons, the land and God's sanctuary (Jubilees 25:14–23), a blessing Genesis never gives a mother. Isaac's stolen blessing adds the blessings of Abraham (Jubilees 26:24). Isaac's last blessings, by "a spirit of prophecy," go to Levi and Judah (Jubilees 31:12–20), and Jacob learns they are written on the heavenly tablets (Jubilees 31:32). Every blessing ends with the promise to Abraham: "Whoever blesses you, blessed!" (Genesis 12:3; Genesis 27:29).

sections.b: In Jubilees Isaac lives first at the Well of the Vision, then in Gerar and at the Well of the Oath, and finally in Abraham's tower at Hebron (Jubilees 24:1–21; Jubilees 29:17–19). His lie about Rebekah is left out (compare Genesis 26:6–11), his treaty with Abimelech becomes a forced oath that ends in a curse on the Philistines (Jubilees 24:27–33), and his blessing of Jacob is guided by heaven (Jubilees 26:18). He comforts Rebekah tenderly (Jubilees 27:14–17), regains his sight to see Levi and Judah, and blesses them by a spirit of prophecy at 165 (Jubilees 31:9–27).

sections.b: Jubilees 27:19–27 retells Genesis 28:10–22 and dates the dream to the first day of the first month. The Ge'ez calls the stairway mäʿarg, "a way up," and says the Lord stood "on it" and that the angels were "the angels of the Lord." Jacob calls the place "the house of the Lord" and vows a tenth, which he pays in Jubilees 32.

Rebekah prays that Jacob's sons may be "as many as the months of the year" (Jubilees 25:16). Jubilees 28:11–24 then dates each birth by day, month, year and week of the forty-fourth jubilee: from Reuben in year 2122 from creation to Zebulun, Dinah and Joseph in 2134. Taken as written the dates put Dan before Judah; R. H. Charles (1902) thought several were corrupt. Levi is born on New Year's Day. Benjamin's birth follows in Jubilees 32.
